title: Undo Buffer for Document Editor
business: Software developers building collaborative text editing applications.
problem: Users frequently make accidental deletions or formatting errors, leading to data loss and frustration when no mechanism exists to revert recent actions.
solution: A stack data structure manages the history of user actions by storing state snapshots in a last-in, first-out order, allowing the application to pop the most recent change to restore the previous document state.
steps: Initialize an empty stack to hold document state snapshots.
Push the current document state onto the stack whenever a user performs a significant action.
When an undo command is triggered, pop the top state from the stack.
Apply the popped state to the document view to revert the change.
outcome: Users gain a reliable mechanism to recover from errors, significantly improving the perceived safety and usability of the editing interface.
limitation: Memory consumption grows linearly with the number of stored states; developers must implement a maximum stack depth to prevent memory exhaustion.

questions.question: In Undo Buffer for Document Editor, how does the stack solve the problem of accidental data loss?
options: By storing snapshots in a last-in, first-out order to allow reverting recent actions.
By automatically saving every keystroke to a permanent database file.
By using a FIFO queue to process all user actions in chronological order.
By deleting the most recent action to save memory space.
questions.explanation: The stack structure naturally supports undo functionality by providing access to the most recently added state first.
questions.evidence: A stack data structure manages the history of user actions by storing state snapshots in a last-in, first-out order, allowing the application to pop the most recent change to restore the previous document state.

questions.question: In Undo Buffer for Document Editor, what is the primary trade-off when using a stack for history management?
options: The stack requires constant re-indexing of all stored document states.
Memory usage increases with history size, requiring a maximum stack depth.
The stack cannot handle more than two undo operations at any time.
Undo operations become slower as the stack size decreases.
questions.explanation: Because stacks store state snapshots, they consume memory; without a limit, they can cause memory exhaustion.
questions.evidence: Memory consumption grows linearly with the number of stored states; developers must implement a maximum stack depth to prevent memory exhaustion.
